# bgraph reference

<!-- Generated by `bgraph docs`. Edit src/docgen.rs, not this file. -->

Diagrams as text, where **you** decide the layout.

Mermaid and friends auto-place everything and leave you fighting the engine.
`bgraph` inverts that: every node says where it goes, but says it *relative to
its neighbours* — so you keep control without hand-editing coordinates every
time the diagram grows.

- A prose introduction lives in [`../README.md`](../README.md).
- A worked tour of the syntax lives in [`language.md`](language.md).
- **This file is the exhaustive reference**, generated from the compiler's own
  tables, so it always describes the binary you have.

## Commands

```
bgraph diagram.bd -o diagram.svg    # render
bgraph diagram.bd -o diagram.png    # …with the `png` feature; --scale 2 for twice the size
bgraph diagram.bd -o diagram.json   # the solved geometry, for another program
bgraph diagram.bd -o d.svg --embed-font Inter.ttf   # text exact on any machine
bgraph diagram.bd -o big.pdf --page a4  # tile a large diagram across sheets
bgraph diagram.bd --theme dark      # a named palette under the file's own styles
bgraph watch diagram.bd             # show it, and reload when it changes
bgraph watch diagram.svg            # …a picture works too; the extension decides
bgraph watch diagram.bd --server    # …the browser preview rather than a window
bgraph watch diagram.bd --port 9000
bgraph watch docs/diagrams          # a directory: build every .bd as it changes
bgraph watch docs/diagrams --once   # …once, non-zero on failure — a build step
bgraph check diagram.bd             # diagnostics only; non-zero on error
bgraph check diagram.bd --ci        # …the flat form, whatever stdout is
bgraph diff old.bd new.bd -o d.svg  # what appeared, what left, what moved
bgraph explain diagram.bd api     # why that box is where it is
bgraph layout diagram.bd            # write the placements in; the picture is unchanged
bgraph report.bd --data q3.json     # fill a template's holes from JSON
bgraph report.bd --set year=2026    # …or bind a scalar on the command line
bgraph report.bd --rows r=sales.csv # …or one hole from the rows of a CSV
bgraph watch report.bd --data q3.json  # live preview of a filled template
bgraph fmt diagram.bd               # reformat; --check reports instead
bgraph fmt --migrate old.bd         # a removed `opacity` becomes the colour's alpha
bgraph init pie                     # a working file for a genre; no genre lists them
bgraph completions fish             # a completion script; bash|zsh|fish|elvish|powershell
bgraph completions man              # …or the man page, from the same flags
bgraph docs -o docs/reference.md    # regenerate this file
bgraph-lsp                          # language server, LSP over stdin/stdout
```

The watch page reloads on every save and reports parse and layout errors in
place, so a broken file never costs you the preview. Scroll to zoom, drag to
pan, `f` to fit, `0` for actual size — and the view survives the reload, or
zooming while editing would be pointless.

## The five statements

```
type <archetype> { … }      // the genre of diagram; optional, defaults to free
graph { … }                 // diagram-wide settings
style <name> [extends <name>] { … }
group <id> ["<label>"] [.class …] [<placement>] { … }
activate <id> { … }         // type sequence: a bar down an existing lifeline
<keyword> <id> ["<label>"] <data…> [.class …] [<placement>] { … }
<id> <arrow> <id> ["<label>"] [.class …] { … }
```

The fourth is an **item**, and each archetype has its own word for it —
`node` in `free`, `slice` in `pie`, `field` in `packet`. `node` stays a
universal synonym everywhere, so nothing is ever forced.

```
type pie
slice organic "Organic search" 4820
slice referral 1180                    // no label: the id is displayed
node b "Direct" { value: 2410 }        // the long form, still valid
```

Values after the label fill the archetype's slots in order, and are **sugar
for the properties it declares** — `slice a 4820` and `slice a { value: 4820 }`
build the same thing. The first string after the identifier is always the
label, so an archetype whose data is a string obliges you to write one.

A statement runs to its separator. `node a node b` on one line is therefore
one item with two stray values, not two items, and `check` says so.

Statements are separated by newlines; `;` and `,` also work. Comments start
with `//` — `#` is reserved for hex colors and cannot also open a comment.

Identifiers may contain letters, digits, `_` and an interior `-`. A trailing
hyphen is not allowed, which is what lets `a->b` split into three tokens.
The four statement keywords — `type`, `graph`, `style`, `node` — are reserved
and cannot name a node.

Labels are quoted. `\n` splits a label into centred lines; `\t` and `\"` also
work. A node with no label falls back to its identifier. Label text is
XML-escaped on output, so `<`, `&` and quotes are safe.

## Groups

A `group` is a frame. Its block holds properties *and* nested statements, so
groups nest:

```
group edge "Edge" {
  padding: 22
  node gw   "Gateway"
  node auth "Auth" below gw gap 30
}

group core "Core" right-of edge gap 60 {
  node orders "Orders"
}

node db "Postgres" right-of core gap 60
```

**A group is sized by its members, never the other way round** — its rectangle
is their bounding box plus its `padding`. That keeps the rule this language is
built on: the items say where they go.

A group may still carry a placement, and then it **translates its whole
subtree** once its members have landed. Members of a placed group only become
anchorable after that translation, so nothing outside can latch onto a
position that is about to move.

Groups and items share one namespace, so a group can be anchored to by name.
An edge to a group is refused — a frame has no obvious endpoint. Style them
with `style group { … }` or a `.class`; the default is a dashed border, a
transparent fill and the label set into the top-left.

## Placement

| Form | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `at (x, y)` | absolute top-left corner |
| `right-of <id>` | to the right of another node |
| `left-of <id>` | to its left |
| `below <id>` | underneath it |
| `above <id>` | over it |
| `gap <n>` | distance to the anchor; defaults to the graph `gap` |
| `align <kw>` | cross-axis alignment against the anchor |

Anchors may point **forward**: the solver runs repeated passes, so a node may
be anchored to one declared later. A genuine loop is reported as an error.

A node with no placement flows from the previous one in source order, using
the graph's `flow` direction and `gap`. The first node lands at `(0, 0)`.

Sizes come from the label plus `padding` unless `size`, `width` or `height`
says otherwise. The canvas is derived from the content — nothing is ever
clipped, and negative coordinates are fine.

## Arrows

| Token | Line | Heads |
|---|---|---|
| `->` | solid | end |
| `<-` | solid | start |
| `<->` | solid | both |
| `--` | solid | none |
| `-->` | dashed | end |
| `..>` | dotted | end |
| `..` | dotted | none |

The token's dash pattern is a default; `{ dash: solid }` overrides it.

## Colors

`#rgb`, `#rgba`, `#rrggbb`, `#rrggbbaa`, or an SVG color name (`white`,
`tomato`).

**The fourth channel is the alpha**, and it defaults to `ff` — opaque. There
is no separate `opacity` property: transparency belongs to the color that
carries it, which is what lets a shape have an opaque border and a translucent
fill.

```
node card "Card" {
  fill: #1e293b80      // half-transparent slate
  stroke: #38bdf8      // fully opaque, alpha omitted
  font-color: #e2e8f0c0
}
```

On output the alpha becomes its own attribute — `fill="#1e293b" fill-opacity="0.5"`
rather than an eight-digit hex. Both render identically in a modern viewer, but
several SVG-to-PDF paths and older renderers drop the inline alpha silently.

Note that this is per-paint, not per-element: a translucent fill lets the inner
half of a thick stroke show through, which a single element opacity would have
composited away first.

## The style cascade

```
built-in defaults  →  style node / style edge  →  .classes (in order)  →  inline { }
```

The implicit theme is the archetype's own word — `style slice { … }` in a
pie — with `style node` and `style edge` remaining universal aliases, applied
first so the specific name wins where both are declared. `extends` flattens a chain
child-first. An unknown property or an unknown `.class` is an error.

## Property reference

Every property below is valid on a `style` block, on a `node` or edge statement's inline block, or both. Anything else is an error, not a silent no-op — a typo surfaces the moment you save.

Aliases are marked. They behave identically to the property they alias; the editor keeps them out of completion so the list stays short.

| Property | Applies to | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `legend` | both | `legend: <text>` | What this style class is called in a `legend` statement. Its presence is what puts the class in one — a legend built from every class would list the ones that only round a corner, and one built from the colours in use would have nothing to call them. |
| `description` | both | `description: <text>` | What this is, in a sentence. Emitted as an SVG `<title>` in every genre — a tooltip to a reader with a mouse, a label to one with a screen reader — and additionally *drawn* under the technology line in `type block`, which has room for it. |
| `desc` *(alias)* | both | `desc: <text>` | Alias for `description`. |
| `fill` | node | `fill: <color>` | Interior color of the shape. |
| `background` *(alias)* | node | `background: <color>` | Alias of `fill`. |
| `stroke` | both | `stroke: <color> <width> <solid\|dashed\|dotted>` | Outline. Accepts a color, a width and a dash pattern in any order; omit whichever you don't need. |
| `border` *(alias)* | both | `border: <color> <width> <pattern>` | Alias of `stroke`. |
| `color` *(alias)* | both | `color: <color> <width> <pattern>` | Alias of `stroke`. For text color use `font-color`. |
| `stroke-width` | both | `stroke-width: <number>` | Outline thickness in user units. |
| `weight` *(alias)* | both | `weight: <number>` | Alias of `stroke-width`. |
| `dash` | both | `dash: <solid\|dashed\|dotted> \| dash: <on> <off>` | Dash pattern. Named, or explicit on/off lengths such as `dash: 6 3`. |
| `radius` | node | `radius: <number>` | Corner rounding — applies to the `rect` shape. |
| `corner` *(alias)* | node | `corner: <number>` | Alias of `radius`. |
| `shape` | node | `shape: <rect\|stadium\|ellipse\|diamond\|hexagon\|cylinder>` | Outline geometry. Edge endpoints are clipped against it. |
| `size` | node | `size: <width> <height>` | Fixed size. Without it the box is sized from the label and `padding`. |
| `width` | node | `width: <number>` | Fixed width; the height still follows the label. |
| `height` | node | `height: <number>` | Fixed height; the width still follows the label. |
| `padding` | node | `padding: <number>` | Inset between the label and the outline; drives the auto-size. |
| `font` | both | `font: <size> "<family>" <color> <weight>` | Shorthand read by value kind, so the order is free: a number is the size, a string the family, a color the ink, a bare word the weight. |
| `font-size` | both | `font-size: <number>` | Text size in user units. |
| `font-family` | both | `font-family: "<family>"` | Font stack, emitted verbatim into the SVG. |
| `font-color` | both | `font-color: <color>` | Text color. |
| `text-color` *(alias)* | both | `text-color: <color>` | Alias of `font-color`. |
| `font-weight` | both | `font-weight: <weight>` | Any SVG weight — `400`, `bold`, `600`… |
| `label-offset` | both | `label-offset: <dx> <dy>` | Move the text by hand, in user units — positive is right and down. `dy` may be omitted. On an edge it also **pins** the label: the automatic avoidance stops moving it, and the offset is measured from the middle of the line. |
| `text-offset` *(alias)* | both | `text-offset: <dx> <dy>` | Alias of `label-offset`. |
| `arrow` | edge | `arrow: <solid\|open\|dot\|none>` | Arrow head style. The arrow token decides which ends carry one. |
| `head` *(alias)* | edge | `head: <solid\|open\|dot\|none>` | Alias of `arrow`. |
| `router` | edge | `router: <straight\|ortho>` | `straight` draws a direct line; `ortho` draws a right-angled elbow. |
| `route` *(alias)* | edge | `route: <straight\|ortho>` | Alias of `router`. |
| `shadow` | node | `shadow: <on\|off>` | Soft drop shadow under the shape. |

## Graph settings

Declared once, in `graph { … }`. These are diagram-wide and are not part of the style cascade.

| Setting | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `description` | `description: <text>` | What the diagram is, in a sentence, for a reader who cannot see it. Becomes `aria-label` on the SVG root, beside `role="img"`. |
| `title` | `title: <text>` | Heading drawn above the diagram. Every genre accepts it here — the chart archetypes also take a `title` in their own settings, and that one wins where both are given. |
| `padding` | `padding: <number>` | Margin between the drawing and the canvas edge. |
| `sketch` | `sketch: <on\|off>` | Draw as if by hand. A sketched architecture says "this is a proposal" where a crisp one says "this is decided" — information rather than ornament. Deterministic: the wobble is a hash of each shape's own geometry, so the same file always produces the same file. |
| `grid` | `grid: <number> <number>` | Column and row step for `at (col 3, row 2)`. One number sets both. A coordinate system, not a solver: nothing is snapped to it, and a box placed in pixels is unaffected. |
| `gap` | `gap: <number>` | Default distance used by anchors that omit `gap`. |
| `background` | `background: <color>` | Canvas fill. Also backs edge labels so they stay readable. |
| `bg` *(alias)* | `bg: <color>` | Alias of `background`. |
| `flow` | `flow: <right\|left\|down\|up>` | Direction used to place nodes that declare no placement. |
| `direction` *(alias)* | `direction: <right\|left\|down\|up>` | Alias of `flow`. |

The surface is **explicit by default**: without a `background` the renderer still paints `#ffffff`, so the live preview and the exported file agree. Write `background: none` (or `transparent`) for a transparent SVG — the preview then shows a checkerboard rather than pretending.

## Archetypes

`type` picks the genre of diagram, once, at the top of the file. Without it the file is `free`.

Every archetype reads the *same* statements: a `node` is a box, a slice or a bitfield depending on the genre. The style cascade, the diagnostics and the editor support are identical in all of them — what changes is which properties carry meaning.

### `type free`

Nodes and edges placed by anchors — the default when a file declares no `type`.

```
node <id> ["label"]
```

It takes no settings.

<details>
<summary>A complete file — <code>examples/groups.bd</code></summary>

```
// A group is a frame sized by what it holds. Give it a placement and the
// whole subtree moves together.

graph { background: #0f172a padding: 32 gap: 44 }

style node  { fill: #1e293b stroke: #334155 1.5 font: 13 #e2e8f0 radius: 8 }
style group { stroke: #38bdf8 1.2 font: 12 #38bdf8 fill: #38bdf80c radius: 12 }
style edge  { stroke: #64748b 1.5 font: 11 #94a3b8 }
style store extends node { shape: cylinder stroke: #10b981 1.5 }

node client "Client" at (0, 0)

group edge "Edge" right-of client gap 60 {
  padding: 20
  node gw   "Gateway"
  node auth "Auth" below gw gap 26
}

group core "Core services" right-of edge gap 60 {
  padding: 20
  node orders  "Orders"
  node billing "Billing" below orders gap 26
}

node db "Postgres" .store right-of core gap 60

client -> gw    "https"
gw     -> auth  "verify"
gw     -> orders
orders -> billing
orders -> db    "sql"
```

</details>

### `type pie`

A pie or donut chart. Each slice needs a value; its `fill` overrides the automatic palette.

```
slice <id> ["label"] <value>
```

| Setting | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `from` | `from: "<file.csv>"` | Read the slices from a CSV, resolved relative to this file. The header names the columns: `name` (or `label`) and `value`. Carries a consequence worth knowing — a file that reads the disk at render time is no longer autonomous, so `check` can pass and the render still fail. |
| `top` | `top: <number>` | Keep the largest n slices and fold the rest into one. The palette has eight colours and `check` already advises this when a pie has more; `top` is what lets the file do it instead of someone doing the arithmetic by hand outside the tool. |
| `other` | `other: <text>` | What the folded slice is called. `"Other"` unless the file says otherwise. |
| `title` | `title: <text>` | Heading drawn above the chart. |
| `radius` | `radius: <number>` | Outer radius in user units. |
| `donut` | `donut: <0..1>` | Inner hole as a fraction of the radius. `0` is a full pie. |
| `start` | `start: <degrees>` | Angle the first slice starts at. `0` is twelve o'clock. |
| `labels` | `labels: <percent\|value\|both\|none>` | What to write on each slice. Slices too thin to read are skipped. |
| `legend` | `legend: <on\|off>` | Swatch-and-name list beside the chart. On by default — identity must never rest on color alone. |

On a `slice` — these are its own, and are not offered elsewhere:

| Property | Where | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `value` | node | `value: <number>` | Magnitude of a slice. Usually written positionally — `slice emea "EMEA" 4820`. |

<details>
<summary>A complete file — <code>examples/pie.bd</code></summary>

```
type pie {
  title: "Traffic sources"
  radius: 130
  donut: 0.55
  labels: percent
}

graph { background: #0b1120 padding: 32 }

// `slice <id> ["label"] <value>` — the value rides in position.
slice organic  "Organic search" 4820
slice direct   "Direct"         2410
slice referral "Referral"       1180
slice social   "Social"          690
slice paid     "Paid"            410
```

</details>

### `type gantt`

Bars on a calendar. A task says when it starts and either when it ends or how long it runs; a `group` becomes a section.

```
task <id> ["label"] <start> <start>
```

| Setting | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | `title: <text>` | Heading drawn above the chart. |
| `size` | `size: <width> <row height>` | How wide the calendar runs and how tall one task is. |
| `ticks` | `ticks: <day\|week\|month>` | How often the calendar is marked. Chosen from the span if unset. |
| `today` | `today: <date>` | Draws a line at one date, for reading progress against it. |

On a `task` — these are its own, and are not offered elsewhere:

| Property | Where | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `start` | node | `start: <date> <date\|duration>` | When a task begins, and either when it ends or how long it runs — read by value kind. |
| `length` | node | `length: <duration>` | How long a task runs, when the start is given on its own. |

<details>
<summary>A complete file — <code>examples/gantt.bd</code></summary>

```
type gantt {
  title: "bgraph, the archetypes"
  size: 560 26
  today: 2026-09-14
}
graph { background: #0b1120 padding: 32 }
style task  { font: 12 #e2e8f0 }
style group { stroke: #334155 1 font: 11 #94a3b8 fill: #ffffff06 radius: 4 }

group found "foundations" {
  task vocab  "vocabulary"   2026-08-03 6d
  task groups "containers"   2026-08-09 5d
  task frame  "plot frame"   2026-08-14 4d
  task dates  "dates"        2026-08-18 3d
}

group charts "charts" {
  task pie  "pie"      2026-08-21 3d
  task bars "bar & xy" 2026-08-24 6d
  task tree "treemap"  2026-08-30 4d
  task flow "sankey"   2026-09-03 5d
}

group dev "software" {
  task seq   "sequence" 2026-09-08 5d
  task state "state"    2026-09-13 4d
  task uml   "class"    2026-09-17 4d
  task plan  "gantt"    2026-09-21 2026-09-28
}
```

</details>

### `type class`

Boxes with a name and a list of members, placed by anchors like `free`. A bare string in the block is a member.

```
class <id> ["label"]
```

| Setting | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | `title: <text>` | Heading drawn above the diagram. |

<details>
<summary>A complete file — <code>examples/class.bd</code></summary>

```
type class { title: "Ordering domain" }
graph { background: #0b1120 padding: 32 gap: 56 }

style class { fill: #1e293b stroke: #38bdf8 1.4 font: 13 #e2e8f0 radius: 6 padding: 14 }
style edge  { stroke: #64748b 1.4 font: 11 #94a3b8 }

class user "User" at (0, 0) {
  - id: Uuid
  - email: String
  - name: String
}

class order "Order" right-of user gap 90 {
  - id: Uuid
  - user_id: Uuid
  - total: Money
  - placed_at: DateTime
}

class line "OrderLine" below order gap 44 {
  - order_id: Uuid
  - sku: String
  - qty: u32
}

class money "Money" right-of order gap 90 {
  - amount: i64
  - currency: Iso4217
}

user  -> order "places"
order -> line  "contains"
order -> money "totals" { dash: dashed }
```

</details>

### `type timeline`

Events on a date line. Each event needs a date; they are drawn in date order with their labels staggered above and below, so a cluster of dates stays readable without hand-placing anything.

```
event <id> ["label"] <date>
```

| Setting | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | `title: <text>` | Heading drawn above the diagram. |
| `size` | `size: <width> <row-height>` | How wide the date line runs, and how much room one row of staggered labels takes. |
| `ticks` | `ticks: <day\|week\|month\|year>` | How often the axis is labelled. Chosen from the span when it is not declared. |

On an `event` — these are its own, and are not offered elsewhere:

| Property | Where | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `date` | node | `date: <date>` | When the event happened. Usually written positionally — `event launch "Launch" 2026-03-15`. Events are drawn in date order, and their labels staggered above and below the line so a cluster stays readable. |

<details>
<summary>A complete file — <code>examples/timeline.bd</code></summary>

```
type timeline { title: "Rust editions and releases" size: 860 36 }
graph { background: #ffffff padding: 32 }

event r1  "Rust 1.0"        2015-05-15
event e15 "Edition 2015"    2015-05-15
event e18 "Edition 2018"    2018-12-06
event async "async/await"   2019-11-07
event e21 "Edition 2021"    2021-10-21
event gats "GATs stabilised" 2022-11-03
event lets "let-else"       2022-06-30
event e24 "Edition 2024"    2025-02-20
```

</details>

### `type block`

Architecture and C4-style component views: typed elements with a technology and a description, nested with `group`, joined by relations that carry a protocol. Placed by anchors exactly as in `free` — the archetype supplies the vocabulary and the shapes.

```
block <id> ["label"] <kind>
```

| Setting | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | `title: <text>` | Heading drawn above the diagram. |

On a `block` — these are its own, and are not offered elsewhere:

| Property | Where | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `kind` | node | `kind: <person\|system\|container\|component\|database\|queue\|external>` | What this element is. Usually written positionally — `block api "API" container`. `external` draws a dashed, muted box for something outside the system being described. |
| `tech` | both | `tech: <text>` | The technology, drawn in brackets under the name — `[Container: Rust]`. On an edge it reads as the protocol: `web -> api "reads" { tech: "HTTPS/JSON" }`. |
| `technology` *(alias)* | both | `technology: <text>` | Alias of `tech`. |

<details>
<summary>A complete file — <code>examples/block.bd</code></summary>

```
type block { title: "Internet banking — containers" }
graph { background: #f8fafc padding: 36 gap: 72 }

block customer "Personal Banking Customer" person {
  description: "A customer of the bank, with personal accounts."
}

group system "Internet Banking System" below customer gap 52 {
  block web "Web Application" container at (0, 0) {
    tech: "Java, Spring MVC"
    description: "Delivers the static content and the SPA."
  }
  block spa "Single-Page App" container right-of web gap 150 {
    tech: "TypeScript, Angular"
    description: "Provides all the banking functionality in the browser."
  }
  block api "API Application" container below spa gap 64 {
    tech: "Java, Spring MVC"
    description: "Provides banking functionality via a JSON/HTTPS API."
  }
  block db "Database" database left-of api gap 150 {
    tech: "Oracle 19c"
    description: "Stores user registration, hashed credentials and logs."
  }
}

block mainframe "Mainframe Banking System" external below db gap 56 {
  description: "Stores the core banking information."
}

customer -> web "Visits bigbank.com" { tech: "HTTPS" }
web -> spa "Delivers to the browser"
spa -> api "Makes API calls to" { tech: "JSON/HTTPS" }
api -> db "Reads from and writes to" { tech: "SQL/TCP" }
api -> mainframe "Makes API calls to" { tech: "XML/HTTPS" }
```

</details>

### `type er`

Entities and the relations between them. A bare string in the block is a column, exactly as in `class`; what `er` adds is cardinality at each end of a relation, written after the label and read at the end nearest the entity it describes — `order -> line "contains" one many` is one order, many lines.

```
entity <id> ["label"]
```

```
<from> -> <to> ["label"] <from-card> <to-card>
```

| Setting | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | `title: <text>` | Heading drawn above the diagram. |

On an `entity` — these are its own, and are not offered elsewhere:

| Property | Where | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `from-card` | edge | `from-card: <one\|many\|zero-one\|zero-many\|one-many>` | Cardinality at the tail of a relation, drawn as a crow's foot against that entity. Usually written positionally — `order -> line "contains" one many`. |
| `to-card` | edge | `to-card: <one\|many\|zero-one\|zero-many\|one-many>` | Cardinality at the head of a relation. A declared cardinality replaces the arrowhead at that end. |

<details>
<summary>A complete file — <code>examples/er.bd</code></summary>

```
type er { title: "Ordering schema" }
graph { background: #0b1120 padding: 32 gap: 56 }

style entity { fill: #1e293b stroke: #38bdf8 1.4 font: 13 #e2e8f0 radius: 6 padding: 14 }
style edge   { stroke: #64748b 1.4 font: 11 #94a3b8 head: none }

entity customer "Customer" at (0, 0) {
  - id: uuid PK
  - email: text
  - created_at: timestamptz
}

entity order "Order" right-of customer gap 120 {
  - id: uuid PK
  - customer_id: uuid FK
  - placed_at: timestamptz
  - total_cents: bigint
}

entity line "OrderLine" below order gap 56 {
  - order_id: uuid FK
  - sku: text
  - qty: integer
}

entity address "Address" below customer gap 56 {
  - customer_id: uuid FK
  - line1: text
  - city: text
}

customer -> order   "places"    one many
order    -> line    "contains"  one one-many
customer -> address "ships to"  one zero-many
```

</details>

### `type state`

A state machine. States are placed by anchors, exactly as in `free` — the archetype supplies the vocabulary and the shapes, not a layout engine. Nest them with `group`.

```
state <id> ["label"]
```

| Setting | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | `title: <text>` | Heading drawn above the machine. |

On a `state` — these are its own, and are not offered elsewhere:

| Property | Where | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `kind` | node | `kind: <state\|initial\|final\|choice>` | What a state is. `initial` and `final` are drawn as marks rather than boxes and take no label; `choice` is a decision diamond. |
| `guard` | edge | `guard: <text>` | A condition on a transition, shown in brackets after its label. |

<details>
<summary>A complete file — <code>examples/state.bd</code></summary>

```
type state { title: "Order lifecycle" }
graph { background: #0b1120 padding: 32 gap: 54 }

style state { fill: #1e293b stroke: #38bdf8 1.5 font: 13 #e2e8f0 padding: 16 }
style edge  { stroke: #64748b 1.5 font: 11 #94a3b8 }
style group { stroke: #f59e0b 1.2 font: 11 #f59e0b fill: #f59e0b0c }

state begin      { kind: initial }
state draft "Draft"        right-of begin gap 46
state placed "Placed"      right-of draft

group fulfil "fulfilment" {
  padding: 22
  state picking "Picking"  right-of placed gap 60
  state shipped "Shipped"  right-of picking gap 46
}

state done "Delivered"     right-of fulfil gap 56
state stop { kind: final }  right-of done gap 46
state cancelled "Cancelled" below placed gap 62

begin   -> draft
draft   -> placed  "submit"
placed  -> picking "pay"      { guard: "funds cleared" }
picking -> shipped "dispatch"
shipped -> done    "deliver"
done    -> stop
placed  -> cancelled "cancel"
```

</details>

### `type sequence`

Participants across the top, messages down the page in the order they are written. A `group` frames the messages inside it.

```
participant <id> ["label"]
```

| Setting | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | `title: <text>` | Heading drawn above the diagram. |
| `column` | `column: <number>` | Width of a participant's column. 150 by default. |
| `row` | `row: <number>` | Vertical space one message takes. 46 by default. |
| `numbered` | `numbered: <on\|off>` | Number the messages in order. |

<details>
<summary>A complete file — <code>examples/sequence.bd</code></summary>

```
type sequence {
  title: "Checkout"
  column: 160
  row: 46
  numbered: on
}
graph { background: #0b1120 padding: 30 }
style participant { fill: #1e293b stroke: #334155 1.5 font: 13 #e2e8f0 radius: 8 }
style edge  { stroke: #7dd3fc 1.5 font: 11 #cbd5e1 }
style group { stroke: #f59e0b 1.2 font: 11 #f59e0b fill: #f59e0b10 }

participant browser "Browser"
participant api     "API"
participant bank    "Bank"
participant db      "Postgres"

browser -> api  "POST /checkout"

// The box down `api`'s lifeline while the call is outstanding (W-047).
activate api {
  api -> db   "reserve stock"
  db  --> api "ok"
}

group retry "retry up to 3×" {
  api  -> bank "authorise"
  bank --> api "declined" { stroke: #f43f5e }
}

api  -> bank "authorise"
bank --> api "approved"
api  -> db   "commit"
api  --> browser "201 Created"
```

</details>

### `type xy`

Lines, areas or dots over a shared x axis. One series per statement, its numbers evenly spaced across the plot — or `scatter`, which reads coordinates instead.

```
series <id> ["label"] <points> …
```

```
scatter <id> ["label"] <pairs> …
```

The same plot, read as coordinates: values are taken two at a time, so `scatter north 1 4 3 8` places points at (1, 4) and (3, 8). Its x values are the ones written, not the position in the line — which is the whole difference from `series`.

| Setting | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | `title: <text>` | Heading drawn above the chart. |
| `size` | `size: <width> <height>` | The plot area, before axis labels and legend. 560 by 320 by default. |
| `categories` | `categories: "<first>" "<second>" …` | Labels for the x positions. One per point, in order. |
| `x-axis` | `x-axis: <min> <max>` | A numeric x span instead of named categories; the points are spread evenly across it. |
| `y-axis` | `y-axis: <min> <max>` | Force the value axis. Otherwise it is rounded outward from the data to human numbers. |
| `mark` | `mark: <line\|area\|dot>` | How a series is drawn. `line` by default; `area` fills beneath it, `dot` plots the points alone. |
| `legend` | `legend: <on\|off>` | Swatch-and-name list. Shown from two series up. |

On a `series` — these are its own, and are not offered elsewhere:

| Property | Where | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `points` | node | `points: <n> <n> …` | One number per step, spread evenly across the x axis. Usually written positionally — `series north 4 8 15`. |
| `pairs` | node | `pairs: <x> <y> <x> <y> …` | Coordinates, read two at a time — the shape `scatter` carries. `scatter north 1 4 3 8` is two points, at (1, 4) and (3, 8). An odd count is an error: the last x would have no y. |

<details>
<summary>A complete file — <code>examples/xy.bd</code></summary>

```
type xy {
  title: "Requests per second, by week"
  size: 520 260
  categories: "W1" "W2" "W3" "W4" "W5" "W6" "W7" "W8"
  mark: line
}
graph { background: #0b1120 padding: 32 }
style series { font: 12 #e2e8f0 }

series edge   "Edge"    120 168 155 210 265 240 310 355
series origin "Origin"   90 102 118 130 126 148 160 172
series cache  "Cache"    30  66  37  80 139  92 150 183
```

</details>

### `type bar`

Bars grouped or stacked across named categories. One series per statement, its numbers in category order.

```
series <id> ["label"] <points> …
```

| Setting | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | `title: <text>` | Heading drawn above the chart. |
| `size` | `size: <width> <height>` | The plot area, before axis labels and legend. 560 by 320 by default. |
| `categories` | `categories: "<first>" "<second>" …` | What the bars stand along. Each series gives one number per category, in this order. |
| `stack` | `stack: <on\|off>` | Stack the series instead of standing them side by side. |
| `y-axis` | `y-axis: <min> <max>` | Force the value axis. Otherwise it is rounded outward from the data to human numbers. |
| `legend` | `legend: <on\|off>` | Swatch-and-name list. Shown from two series up; identity must never rest on colour alone. |

On a `series` — these are its own, and are not offered elsewhere:

| Property | Where | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `points` | node | `points: <n> <n> …` | One number per category, in order. Usually written positionally — `series north 4 8 15`. |

<details>

  title: "Quarterly revenue, by region"
  size: 520 280
  categories: "Q1" "Q2" "Q3" "Q4"
}

style series { font: 12 #e2e8f0 }

series emea "EMEA"   120 185 240 310

series apac "APAC"    80 130 175 260

### `type sankey`

Flows between stages, sized by magnitude. The value rides on the link, not on what it joins: a node's height is whatever passes through it.

```
node <id> ["label"]
```

```
<from> -> <to> ["label"] <value>
```

| Setting | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | `title: <text>` | Heading drawn above the diagram. |
| `size` | `size: <width> <height>` | The area the flows fill. 680 by 400 by default. |
| `gap` | `gap: <number>` | Space between stacked nodes in a column. |
| `width` | `width: <number>` | Thickness of a node bar. |
| `labels` | `labels: <name\|value\|both\|none>` | What to write beside each node. |

On a `node` — these are its own, and are not offered elsewhere:

| Property | Where | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `value` | edge | `value: <number>` | How much flows along this link. Usually written positionally — `coal -> grid 40`. |

<details>
<summary>A complete file — <code>examples/sankey.bd</code></summary>

```
type sankey {
  title: "Where the traffic goes"
  size: 620 340
  gap: 16
  labels: both
}
graph { background: #0b1120 padding: 32 }
style node { font: 12 #e2e8f0 }

node search "Organic"
node social "Social"
node paid   "Paid"
node landing "Landing"
node pricing "Pricing"
node signup  "Sign-up"
node bounce  "Bounce"

search  -> landing 4200
social  -> landing 1500
paid    -> pricing  900
search  -> pricing  620
landing -> signup  2100
landing -> bounce  3600
pricing -> signup  1100
pricing -> bounce   420
```

</details>

### `type wave`

A timing diagram. Each signal carries a wave string, one character per period, in the WaveDrom alphabet.

```
signal <id> ["label"] <wave>
```

| Setting | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | `title: <text>` | Heading drawn above the lanes. |
| `period` | `period: <number>` | Width of one wave character. 40 by default. |
| `lane` | `lane: <height> <gap>` | Height of a signal lane and the space beneath it. |
| `ruler` | `ruler: <on\|off>` | Period numbers above the lanes. On by default. |
| `every` | `every: <number>` | Label a ruler tick every N periods. 4 by default. |
| `sketch` | `sketch: <on\|off>` | Draw as if by hand. A sketched architecture says "this is a proposal" where a crisp one says "this is decided" — information rather than ornament. Deterministic: the wobble is a hash of each shape's own geometry, so the same file always produces the same file. |
| `grid` | `grid: <on\|off>` | Vertical lines on the period boundaries. On by default. |

On a `signal` — these are its own, and are not offered elsewhere:

| Property | Where | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `wave` | node | `wave: "<characters>"` | One character per period: `0` `1` `l` `h` levels, `p` `n` clocks, `x` unknown, `z` high-impedance, `=` and `2`–`9` data, `.` repeats the previous, `\|` a gap. |
| `data` | node | `data: "<first>" "<second>" …` | Names for the data segments of a wave, in order. |

<details>
<summary>A complete file — <code>examples/wave.bd</code></summary>

```
type wave {
  title: "SPI transfer"
  period: 34
  lane: 26 16
  every: 1
}
graph { background: #0b1120 padding: 30 }
style signal { font: 12 #e2e8f0 stroke: #7dd3fc }

signal sclk "SCLK"  "p........."
signal cs   "~CS"   "10........1"
signal mosi "MOSI"  "x.=.=.=.=.x" { data: "cmd" "addr" "data" "crc" }
signal miso "MISO"  "z...=.=...z" { data: "ack" "status" }
signal busy "BUSY"  "0..1...0..."
```

</details>

### `type quadrant`

Points on two axes, divided into four named regions. A Wardley map is this archetype with its own axis names.

```
point <id> ["label"] <x> <y>
```

| Setting | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | `title: <text>` | Heading drawn above the chart. |
| `size` | `size: <width> <height>` | The plot area. 460 square by default. |
| `range` | `range: <min> <max>` | The span both axes cover. `0 1` by default. |
| `x-axis` | `x-axis: "<left>" "<right>"` | What the horizontal axis means at each end. |
| `y-axis` | `y-axis: "<bottom>" "<top>"` | What the vertical axis means at each end. |
| `quadrants` | `quadrants: "<top-right>" "<top-left>" "<bottom-left>" "<bottom-right>"` | Names for the four regions, anticlockwise from the top right. |
| `labels` | `labels: <name\|none>` | Whether each point carries its name. |

On a `point` — these are its own, and are not offered elsewhere:

| Property | Where | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `x` | node | `x: <number>` | Horizontal position, on the axis range the archetype declares. |
| `y` | node | `y: <number>` | Vertical position, on the axis range the archetype declares. |

  title: "Where the work sits"
  size: 460 400
  x-axis: "Cheap" "Costly"
  y-axis: "Low value" "High value"
  quadrants: "Do now" "Quick wins" "Drop" "Reconsider"
  labels: name
}
graph { background: #0b1120 padding: 34 }
style point { font: 12 #e2e8f0 }

point wave     "type wave"     0.62 0.86
point sankey   "type sankey"   0.28 0.72
point quadrant "type quadrant" 0.16 0.64
point block    "type block"    0.70 0.55
point gantt    "type gantt"    0.80 0.30

### `type treemap`

Nested rectangles whose area is proportional to a value. The hierarchy is group nesting; a group's area is the sum of what it contains.

```
box <id> ["label"] <value>
```

| Setting | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | `title: <text>` | Heading drawn above the map. |
| `size` | `size: <width> <height>` | The rectangle the map fills. 640 by 400 by default. |
| `gap` | `gap: <number>` | Surface showing between sibling tiles. Adjacent fills must never touch, so this is 2 by default and never 0. |
| `header` | `header: <number>` | Height reserved inside a group's tile for its name. |
| `labels` | `labels: <name\|value\|both\|none>` | What to write on each tile. Tiles too small to read are skipped. |

On a `box` — these are its own, and are not offered elsewhere:

| Property | Where | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `value` | node | `value: <number>` | Area of a box, relative to its siblings. Usually written positionally — `box api "API" 42`. |

<details>
<summary>A complete file — <code>examples/treemap.bd</code></summary>

```
type treemap {
  title: "Repository, by lines of code"
  size: 660 380
  labels: both
}
graph { background: #0b1120 padding: 30 }

group rust "Rust" {
  box lsp    "lsp.rs"        1180
  box charts "charts.rs"      760
  box layout "layout.rs"      620
  box render "render_svg.rs"  560
  box check  "check.rs"       540
  box props  "props.rs"       520
  box tests  "tests.rs"      1240
}

group grammar "Grammar" {
  box pest "syntax.pest"  70
  box ts   "grammar.js"  130
  box corp "corpus"      420
}

group docs "Docs" {
  box ref  "reference.md" 300
  box lang "language.md"  260
  box idx  "INDEX.md"     140
}
```

</details>

### `type packet`

A packet / bitfield diagram. Each field needs an inclusive bit range; one crossing a row boundary is split across rows.

```
field <id> ["label"] <bits> <bits>
```

| Setting | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | `title: <text>` | Heading drawn above the diagram. |
| `width` | `width: <bits>` | Bits per row. 32 by default. |
| `cell` | `cell: <width> <height>` | Width of one bit and the height of a row. |
| `ruler` | `ruler: <on\|off>` | Bit indices above each row. On by default. |

On a `field` — these are its own, and are not offered elsewhere:

| Property | Where | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `bits` | node | `bits: <first> <last>` | Inclusive bit range of a field. `bits: 8` is shorthand for a single bit. Usually written positionally — `field flags "Flags" 8 15`. |

<details>
<summary>A complete file — <code>examples/packet.bd</code></summary>

```
type packet {
  title: "TCP header"
  width: 32
  ruler: on
}

graph { background: #0b1120 }

style field {
  fill: #1e293b
  stroke: #334155 1
  radius: 3
  font: 12 #e2e8f0
}

style flag extends field { fill: #422006 stroke: #f59e0b 1 }

// `field <id> ["label"] <bits> <bits>` — an inclusive range, in position.
field sport "Source port"           0 15
field dport "Destination port"     16 31
field seq   "Sequence number"      32 63
field ack   "Acknowledgment number" 64 95
field off   "Offset"               96 99
field rsv   "Rsvd"                100 102
field flags "Flags" .flag         103 111
field win   "Window"              112 127
field sum   "Checksum"            128 143
field urg   "Urgent pointer"      144 159
```

</details>

### `type gitgraph`

Commits, branches and merges. Parentage is the edges — `c1 -> c2` is c2's parent — and a commit with two parents is a merge. The rails are the archetype's to assign; what the author declares is which branch a commit is on and what came before it.

```
commit <id> ["label"] <branch>
```

| Setting | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | `title: <text>` | Heading drawn above the diagram. |
| `branches` | `branches: "<name>" "<name>" …` | The rails, top to bottom. A commit on a branch not named here gets a rail of its own at the bottom, in the order first seen. |
| `spacing` | `spacing: <along> <between>` | Distance between two commits on a rail, and between two rails. |

On a `commit` — these are its own, and are not offered elsewhere:

| Property | Where | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `branch` | node | `branch: "<name>"` | Which rail the commit sits on. Usually written positionally — `commit c3 "Fix the ruler" "main"`. |
| `tag` | node | `tag: "<name>"` | A label drawn beside the commit — a release, a marker. |

<details>
<summary>A complete file — <code>examples/gitgraph.bd</code></summary>

```
// Parentage is the edges; the rails are the archetype's to assign. The author
// still declares every commit and what came before it (W-049).
type gitgraph {
  title: "A release, with a hotfix"
  branches: "main" "feature" "hotfix"
  spacing: 96 62
}

graph { background: #0b1120 padding: 30 }
style commit { font: 11 #e2e8f0 }

// `commit <id> ["message"] <branch>`
commit c1 "init"        "main"
commit c2 "parser"      "main" { tag: "v0.1" }
commit f1 "scatter"     "feature"
commit f2 "radar"       "feature"
commit c3 "merge"       "main"
commit h1 "fix the U1"  "hotfix"
commit c4 "merge fix"   "main" { tag: "v0.2" }

c1 -> c2
c2 -> f1
f1 -> f2
c2 -> c3
f2 -> c3
c3 -> h1
c3 -> c4
h1 -> c4
```

</details>

### `type orgchart`

Reporting lines, laid out top-down. The hierarchy comes from the edges — `ceo -> cto` — and the archetype places every box, so adding a report never means renumbering anything.

```
position <id> ["label"]
```

| Setting | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | `title: <text>` | Heading drawn above the diagram. |
| `row` | `row: <number>` | Distance between one level and the next. |
| `spacing` | `spacing: <number>` | Distance between two siblings. |

<details>
<summary>A complete file — <code>examples/orgchart.bd</code></summary>

// report never means renumbering anything (W-041).
type orgchart { title: "Broadcast engineering" row: 96 spacing: 26 }
graph { background: #0b1120 padding: 30 }
style position { fill: #1e293b stroke: #38bdf8 1.3 font: 12 #e2e8f0 radius: 6 padding: 12 }

position cto  "CTO"
position plat "Platform lead"
position sig  "DSP lead"
position ops  "Operations lead"
position k8s  "Kubernetes"
position api  "Backend"
position dsp1 "Signal chain"
position dsp2 "Capture"
position noc  "NOC"

cto -> plat
cto -> sig
cto -> ops
plat -> k8s
plat -> api
sig -> dsp1
sig -> dsp2
ops -> noc
```

</details>

### `type mindmap`

A root with branches either side of it. The same tree the orgchart draws, arranged outward instead of downward, so the root stays central however lopsided the tree is.

```

| `title` | `title: <text>` | Heading drawn above the diagram. |
| `row` | `row: <number>` | Distance between one level and the next. |
| `spacing` | `spacing: <number>` | Distance between two siblings. |

The same tree as indented rows, one per line — a file listing, a menu, a taxonomy. Depth is the indent and order is the order written.

### `type harness`

Wiring harnesses. A connector's pins are its member lines — `- 1: +12V` — and a wire is an edge carrying the pin it lands on at each end. Both mechanisms already existed; what this genre adds is that a wire is checked against the pins that are really there (`D-025`).

```
connector <id> ["label"]
```

```
<from> -> <to> ["label"] <wire> <wire>
```

| Setting | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | `title: <text>` | Heading drawn above the diagram. |
| `pin` | `pin: <width> <height>` | Width of a connector body and the height of one pin row. |

On a `connector` — these are its own, and are not offered elsewhere:

| Property | Where | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `wire` | edge | `wire: <from-pin> <to-pin>` | Which pin at each end a wire lands on, by the number the connector declares as a member line (`D-025`). Usually written positionally — `j1 -> j2 "power" 1 3`. |

<details>
<summary>A complete file — <code>examples/harness.bd</code></summary>

```
// A connector's pins are its member lines; a wire is an edge carrying the pin
// it lands on at each end (D-025, W-045).
type harness { title: "Sensor loom — J1 to J2" }
graph { background: #0b1120 padding: 32 gap: 160 }

style connector { fill: #1e293b stroke: #38bdf8 1.4 font: 12 #e2e8f0 radius: 5 padding: 12 }
style edge      { stroke: #64748b 1.3 font: 10 #94a3b8 head: none }
style power     { stroke: #f43f5e 1.6 font: 10 #fda4af head: none }
style ground    { stroke: #64748b 1.6 font: 10 #94a3b8 head: none dash: dashed }

connector j1 "J1 — MOLEX 4-way" at (0, 0) {
  - 1: +12V
  - 2: GND
  - 3: SIG_A
  - 4: SIG_B
}

connector j2 "J2 — JST 6-way" right-of j1 {
  - 1: VCC
  - 2: RETURN
  - 3: IN_A
  - 4: IN_B
  - 5: SHIELD
  - 6: n/c
}

// `<from> -> <to> ["label"] <from-pin> <to-pin>`
j1 -> j2 "power"  .power  1 1
j1 -> j2 "ground" .ground 2 2
j1 -> j2 "sig A"          3 3
j1 -> j2 "sig B"          4 4
```

</details>

### `type venn`

Overlapping sets. Two or three of them: with two, the lens is solved so its **area** is the number you wrote; with three the overlaps are labelled but arranged rather than solved, because three circles cannot in general honour all seven regions at once. Four is refused rather than drawn wrongly.

```
set <id> ["label"] <count>
```

```
<from> -> <to> ["label"] <shared>
```

| Setting | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | `title: <text>` | Heading drawn above the diagram. |
| `radius` | `radius: <number>` | How large the biggest set is drawn. The others are scaled against it by area, not by radius — a circle read as twice the size is one with twice the ink in it. |

On a `set` — these are its own, and are not offered elsewhere:

| Property | Where | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `count` | node | `count: <number>` | How many things are in the set. Not `size`, which is on the shared table and means a box's width and height. Usually written positionally — `set rust "Rust" 120`. |
| `shared` | edge | `shared: <number>` | How many things two sets have in common, written on a link between them — `rust -> embedded 30`. With two sets the lens is solved to that exact area; with three it is labelled but not solved, because three circles cannot in general be arranged to honour all seven regions at once. |

<details>
<summary>A complete file — <code>examples/venn.bd</code></summary>

```
// Three sets. With two the lens is *solved* to the number written; with three
// the overlaps are labelled but arranged, and `check` says so — three circles
// cannot honour all seven regions at once (W-053).
type venn {
  title: "Who reads which diagram"
  radius: 105
}

graph { background: #ffffff padding: 34 }
style set { font: 12 "Archivo" #1a1a1a }

set dev  "Developers" 420
set ops  "Operations" 260
set arch "Architects" 180

// `<from> -> <to> <shared>` — how many things the two sets have in common.
dev  -> ops  120
ops  -> arch  70
dev  -> arch 140
```

</details>

### `type bpmn`

A business process. Tasks, gateways, events, data artefacts and the flows between them, with pools and lanes as `group`s. Placed by anchors exactly as in `free`: the archetype supplies the vocabulary, the shapes and the diagnostics, and the author still says where everything goes. Four words, because four things have four positional shapes (`D-023`) — a task has a kind, an event has a stage and a trigger, a gateway has a gate and a datum has an artefact.

```
task <id> ["label"] <kind>
```

```
event <id> ["label"] <stage> <trigger>
```

Something that happens: `event got "Order received" start message`. The stage comes first and the trigger second, because a stage is what every event has and a trigger is what some do.

```
gateway <id> ["label"] <gate>
```

A branch or a join: `gateway ok "Approved?" exclusive`.

```
data <id> ["label"] <artifact>
```

What the process reads or writes: `data inv "Invoice" object`.

```
<from> -> <to> ["label"] <flow>
```

| Setting | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | `title: <text>` | Heading drawn above the diagram. |

On a `task` — these are its own, and are not offered elsewhere:

| Property | Where | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `kind` | node | `kind: <plain\|user\|service\|script\|manual\|send\|receive\|rule\|subprocess>` | What kind of task it is, drawn as a marker in the corner of the box. `subprocess` takes the `+` instead, and an *expanded* subprocess is a `group`. Usually written positionally — `task check "Check credit" service`. |
| `stage` | node | `stage: <start\|intermediate\|end\|boundary>` | Where the event sits: a thin ring starts, a thick one ends, a double ring is intermediate. `boundary` is the exception — it is not a place in the flow but a place on a task, so it needs `attach`. |
| `trigger` | node | `trigger: <plain\|message\|timer\|error\|signal\|escalation\|conditional\|terminate>` | What makes the event happen, drawn inside the ring. Written second, after the stage — `event due "Overdue" boundary timer`. |
| `attach` | node | `attach: <task>` | The task a `boundary` event sits on. It is placement, declared like every other placement (`D-001`): the event lands on that box's bottom edge, and several on one task spread along it in the order they are written. `label-offset` moves one by hand. |
| `gate` | node | `gate: <exclusive\|parallel\|inclusive\|event\|complex>` | Which gateway it is, drawn as the mark inside the diamond. Usually written positionally — `gateway ok "Approved?" exclusive`. |
| `artifact` | node | `artifact: <object\|store\|input\|output>` | Which data artefact it is. An object is a page with a folded corner, a store is a cylinder; `input` and `output` are objects carrying the arrow that says which way the data went. |
| `flow` | edge | `flow: <sequence\|message\|association\|default\|conditional>` | What the connector means. A sequence flow is a solid arrow, a message flow is dashed with a hollow head, an association is dotted with none. `default` takes the slash and `conditional` the diamond, both at the gateway end. Usually written positionally — `check -> notify "rejected" default`. |

<details>
<summary>A complete file — <code>examples/bpmn.bd</code></summary>

```
// A business process. Four words, because four things have four positional
// shapes: a task has a kind, an event has a stage and a trigger, a gateway has
// a gate, a datum has an artefact. Placement is declared as it is everywhere
// else — the archetype supplies the notation, the author says where it goes.
type bpmn { title: "Expense claim" }
graph { background: #ffffff padding: 36 gap: 40 }

style node  { font: 13 #111827 stroke: #334155 1.2 fill: #ffffff }
style edge  { stroke: #475569 1.3 font: 11 #475569 }
style store { fill: #f1f5f9 }

group filed "Employee" {
  padding: 22

  event submit "Claim submitted" start message
  task  fill   "Fill the form"   user right-of submit gap 44
}

group review "Finance" below filed gap 34 {
  padding: 22

  task    check "Validate receipts" rule at (0, 0)
  gateway ok    "Within policy?"    exclusive right-of check gap 52
  task    pay   "Pay the claim"     service right-of ok gap 52
  task    query "Ask for detail"    send below pay gap 74
  event   done  "Reimbursed"        end right-of pay gap 52
}

// A boundary event sits *on* a task, and says so by naming it. Placement, and
// declared like every other placement.
event late "14 days" boundary timer { attach: pay }

// The form sits between the two participants, on the side the reader's eye
// already travels: to the right of it, both its association and its message
// flow had to double back across the picture.
data claim  "Claim form" object right-of filed gap 40 align top
data ledger "Ledger"     store below done gap 40

submit -> fill
fill   -> check
check  -> ok
ok     -> pay   "within"
ok     -> query "over"    default
query  -> check
pay    -> done
late   -> query

// A message crosses between participants; an association only relates.
fill  -> claim  association
pay   -> ledger association
claim -> check  message
```

</details>

### `type network`

Network topology: hosts, links and the segments that hold them. Placed by anchors exactly as in `free` — the archetype supplies the vocabulary, the shapes and the diagnostics, and a `group` is a segment or a zone.

```
host <id> ["label"] <role>
```

```
<from> -> <to> ["label"] <speed>
```

| Setting | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | `title: <text>` | Heading drawn above the diagram. |

On a `host` — these are its own, and are not offered elsewhere:

| Property | Where | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `role` | node | `role: <server\|switch\|router\|firewall\|storage\|client\|cloud>` | What the box is. Chooses the shape — a reader tells a router from a storage array before reading the label. Usually written positionally — `host fw "Edge firewall" firewall`. |
| `addr` | node | `addr: "<address>"` | An address, drawn on its own line under the name. Kept as text: a diagram has no business validating a CIDR block. |
| `speed` | edge | `speed: "<rate>"` | What the link runs at, drawn in brackets under its label. Usually written positionally — `sw -> srv "uplink" "10 GbE"`. |

<details>
<summary>A complete file — <code>examples/network.bd</code></summary>

```
// Topology: hosts, links and the segments that hold them. The role picks the
// shape; placement stays declared, as in `free` (W-043).
type network { title: "Capture site — edge to core" }
graph { background: #0b1120 padding: 30 gap: 70 }

style host  { fill: #1e293b stroke: #334155 1.2 font: 12 #e2e8f0 radius: 5 }
style edge  { stroke: #64748b 1.3 font: 10 #94a3b8 head: none }
style group { stroke: #334155 1 fill: #0f172a80 radius: 8 dash: dashed font: 11 #94a3b8 }

host net "Internet" cloud at (0, 0)
host fw  "Edge firewall" firewall below net gap 60 { addr: "203.0.113.1" }
host tor "Top-of-rack" switch below fw gap 60 { addr: "10.0.0.1" }

group core "Core segment — 10.0.0.0/24" {
  host proc01 "snds-p01-proc01" server right-of tor gap 90 { addr: "10.0.0.11" }
  host proc02 "snds-p01-proc02" server below proc01 gap 40 { addr: "10.0.0.12" }
  host shelf  "Storage shelf"   storage below proc02 gap 40 { addr: "10.0.0.20" }
}

net -> fw  "uplink" "1 GbE"
fw  -> tor "trunk"  "10 GbE"
tor -> proc01 "" "10 GbE"
tor -> proc02 "" "10 GbE"
tor -> shelf  "" "10 GbE"
```

</details>

### `type rack`

A rack elevation. Units are numbered from 1 at the **bottom**, as a rack is, and a device occupies an inclusive span of them. Empty units are left empty: unlike a packet, a rack with gaps is a rack with room, not a rack that does not add up.

```
device <id> ["label"] <u> <u>
```

| Setting | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | `title: <text>` | Heading drawn above the frame. |
| `units` | `units: <count>` | How tall the frame is, in rack units. 42 by default. |
| `cell` | `cell: <width> <height>` | Width of the frame and the height of one rack unit. |
| `ruler` | `ruler: <on\|off>` | Unit numbers down the rails. On by default. |

On a `device` — these are its own, and are not offered elsewhere:

| Property | Where | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `u` | node | `u: <lowest> <highest>` | The inclusive span of rack units a device occupies, counted from **1 at the bottom** as a rack is. `u: 12` is a single unit. Usually written positionally — `device srv "Compute node" 38 41`. |

<details>
<summary>A complete file — <code>examples/rack.bd</code></summary>

```
// A rack elevation. Units count from 1 at the bottom, as a rack is labelled —
// and a device occupies an inclusive span of them (W-044).
type rack {
  title: "Rack A3 — capture row"
  units: 24
  cell: 280 20
  ruler: on
}

graph { background: #0b1120 padding: 28 }

style device  { fill: #1e293b stroke: #334155 1 radius: 3 font: 12 #e2e8f0 }
style network extends device { fill: #0c2a3e stroke: #38bdf8 1 }
style power   extends device { fill: #422006 stroke: #f59e0b 1 }

// `device <id> ["label"] <lowest> <highest>`
device tor    "Top-of-rack switch"   .network 24 24
device patch  "Patch panel"          .network 23 23
device proc01 "snds-p01-proc01"               19 22
device proc02 "snds-p01-proc02"               15 18
device cap01  "hp-capture02"                  11 14
device store  "Storage shelf"                  6 9
device ups    "UPS"                  .power     1 4
```

</details>

### `type radar`

Axes radiating from a centre, one closed polygon per series. Every axis shares one scale: the shape a reader compares is only meaningful if a ring means the same thing all the way round.

```
series <id> ["label"] <points> …
```

| Setting | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | `title: <text>` | Heading drawn above the diagram. |
| `categories` | `categories: "<name>" "<name>" …` | One axis per name, clockwise from the top, in the order each series writes its numbers. The same word `bar` uses, because it is the same idea: the named slots the numbers line up with. |
| `radius` | `radius: <number>` | Distance from the centre to the outer ring. 140 by default. |
| `range` | `range: <low> <high>` | The scale every axis shares. Taken from the data when it is not written — one scale, because a radar whose axes disagreed about what a ring means would make its shape a lie. |
| `legend` | `legend: <on\|off>` | Name the series beside the diagram. On when there is more than one. |

On a `series` — these are its own, and are not offered elsewhere:

| Property | Where | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `points` | node | `points: <n> <n> …` | One number per category, in order. Usually written positionally — `series north 4 8 15`. |

<details>
<summary>A complete file — <code>examples/radar.bd</code></summary>

```
// Axes radiating from a centre, one closed polygon per series. Every axis
// shares one scale, or the shape a reader compares would be a lie (W-046).
type radar {
  title: "Two engine designs"
  categories: "Power" "Economy" "Range" "Weight" "Cost" "Noise"
  radius: 140
  range: 0 100
}

graph { background: #0b1120 padding: 32 }
style series { font: 11 #cbd5e1 }

series turbo   "Turbocharged"  92 48 70 55 40 45
series electric "Electric"     78 95 52 40 62 96
```

</details>

### `type journey`

A user journey: steps in the order they are taken, and how each actor felt at each one. `group`s are its sections, drawn as a band above the steps they hold. One line per actor, so the place where two people diverge is the thing you see first.

```
step <id> ["label"] <scores> …
```

| Setting | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | `title: <text>` | Heading drawn above the diagram. |
| `actors` | `actors: "<name>" "<name>" …` | Who is being followed through the journey, in the order their scores are written on each step. One line per actor is drawn. |
| `size` | `size: <width> <height>` | How wide the journey runs and how tall the score band is. |
| `range` | `range: <low> <high>` | The score scale. `1 5` by default; the axis is labelled at every whole step, because a satisfaction score has no meaning between two of them. |
| `legend` | `legend: <on\|off>` | Name the actors beside the diagram. On when there is more than one. |

On a `step` — these are its own, and are not offered elsewhere:

| Property | Where | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `scores` | node | `scores: <n> <n> …` | One score per actor, in the order `actors` declares them. Usually written positionally — `step pay "Pay" 2 4`. |

<details>
<summary>A complete file — <code>examples/journey.bd</code></summary>

```
// Steps in the order they are taken, one line per actor — the point being the
// step where two people diverge (W-052).
type journey {
  title: "Returning an order"
  actors: "Customer" "Support agent"
  size: 620 200
  range: 1 5
}

graph { background: #0b1120 padding: 30 }
style step { font: 11 #cbd5e1 }
style group { stroke: #334155 1 fill: #1e293b60 radius: 5 font: 11 #94a3b8 dash: solid }

group find "Find the order" {
  step login  "Sign in"          4 5
  step locate "Locate the order" 3 5
}

group ask "Ask for the return" {
  step form   "Fill the form"    2 4
  step wait   "Wait for a reply" 1 3
}

group close "Close it" {
  step label  "Print the label"  3 4
  step refund "Refund lands"     5 5
}
```

</details>

### `type kanban`

A board: `group`s are its columns, in the order they are declared, and the cards inside each one stack in the order they are declared. A column may carry a `limit`, and a column over it is reported — a board nobody is told is over its limit is a board that is only a picture.

```
card <id> ["label"]
```

| Setting | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | `title: <text>` | Heading drawn above the board. |
| `column` | `column: <width>` | Width of one column. 220 by default. |

On a `card` — these are its own, and are not offered elsewhere:

| Property | Where | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `limit` | node | `limit: <count>` | The work-in-progress limit of a **column** — the number of cards it is allowed to hold. `check` reports a column over its limit, which is the one thing a board is kept for. Written on the `group`, not on a card; on a card it means nothing and is reported as such. |

<details>
<summary>A complete file — <code>examples/kanban.bd</code></summary>

```
// A board: `group`s are the columns, in declaration order, and the cards
// inside stack in declaration order. A column may carry a WIP `limit` (W-050).
type kanban {
  title: "Sprint 14"
  column: 210
}

graph { background: #0b1120 padding: 28 }

style card    { fill: #1e293b stroke: #334155 1 radius: 5 font: 12 #e2e8f0 }
style group   { fill: #0f172a stroke: #1e293b 1 radius: 8 dash: solid font: 12 #94a3b8 }
style blocked extends card { fill: #422006 stroke: #f59e0b 1 }

group todo "To do" {
  card ruler   "Byte-granular ruler for wire formats"
  card venn    "Circle geometry for overlapping sets"
  card metrics "Real font metrics instead of the estimate"
}

// Deliberately over its limit: the warning firing is the point of the genre.
group doing "In progress" {
  limit: 2
  card board "Columns of cards, sized by what they hold"
  card links "Typed relations between requirements"
  card fonts "Measure text instead of guessing at it" .blocked
}

group review "In review" {
  limit: 3
  card scatter "Coordinates instead of positions"
}

group done "Done" {
  card offset "Manual escape hatch out of label placement"
  card bytes  "Wire formats at byte granularity"
}
```

</details>

### `type requirements`

Requirements and the typed links between them. A bare string in the block is a line of the requirement — its identifier, then what it demands — exactly as in `class`. What this genre adds is the relation vocabulary: a link says what it asserts, read tail to head, and is drawn in guillemets on the line. Placement stays declared, as in `free`.

```
requirement <id> ["label"]
```

```
<from> -> <to> ["label"] <link>
```

| Setting | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | `title: <text>` | Heading drawn above the diagram. |

On a `requirement` — these are its own, and are not offered elsewhere:

| Property | Where | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `risk` | node | `risk: <low\|medium\|high>` | How likely this requirement is to go unmet. Drawn under the name, not as a colour — risk is ordinal and the categorical palette would imply it is not. |
| `verify` | node | `verify: <analysis\|demonstration\|inspection\|test>` | How the requirement will be shown to be met. A requirement with no stated method is one nobody has planned to check. |
| `link` | edge | `link: <derive\|satisfy\|verify\|refine\|trace\|copy>` | What the relation asserts, read tail to head — `r2 -> r1 derive` is r2 derives from r1. Drawn in guillemets on the line. Usually written positionally. |

<details>
<summary>A complete file — <code>examples/requirements.bd</code></summary>

```
// `requirements` is a class box with a relation vocabulary: a bare line in the
// block is a line of the requirement, and a link says what it asserts (W-051).
type requirements { title: "Braking system" }
graph { background: #0b1120 padding: 32 gap: 64 }

style requirement { fill: #1e293b stroke: #38bdf8 1.4 font: 13 #e2e8f0 radius: 6 padding: 14 }
style edge        { stroke: #64748b 1.4 font: 11 #94a3b8 head: open dash: dashed }

requirement stop "Stopping distance" at (0, 0) {
  - REQ-001
  - The vehicle shall stop within 40 m from 100 km/h on dry asphalt.
  risk: high
  verify: test
}

requirement fade "Fade resistance" below stop gap 56 {
  - REQ-002
  - Braking performance shall not drop by more than 10% over ten consecutive stops.
  risk: medium
  verify: test
}

requirement pedal "Pedal force" right-of stop gap 150 {
  - REQ-003
  - Full braking shall require no more than 500 N of pedal force.
  risk: low
  verify: demonstration
}

requirement adas "Emergency assist" below pedal gap 56 {
  - REQ-004
  - The assist shall command full braking within 150 ms of a detected obstacle.
  risk: high
  verify: analysis
}

// `<from> -> <to> ["label"] <link>` — read tail to head.
fade  -> stop  derive
pedal -> stop  refine
adas  -> stop  satisfy
adas  -> pedal trace
```

</details>

### `type bytefield`

A wire-format diagram at byte granularity — `packet` with the ruler counting bytes rather than bits. Each field needs an inclusive byte range; one crossing a row boundary is split across rows.

```
field <id> ["label"] <bytes> <bytes>
```

| Setting | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | `title: <text>` | Heading drawn above the diagram. |
| `width` | `width: <bytes>` | Bytes per row. 16 by default — the width a hex dump is read at. |
| `cell` | `cell: <width> <height>` | Width of one byte and the height of a row. |
| `ruler` | `ruler: <on\|off>` | Byte offsets above each row. On by default. |

On a `field` — these are its own, and are not offered elsewhere:

| Property | Where | Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `bytes` | node | `bytes: <first> <last>` | Inclusive byte range of a field. `bytes: 4` is shorthand for a single byte. Usually written positionally — `field magic "Magic" 0 3`, which is four bytes. |

<details>
<summary>A complete file — <code>examples/bytefield.bd</code></summary>

```
// `bytefield` is `packet` read one order of magnitude up: the ruler counts
// bytes, and a field's range is an inclusive byte range (W-039).
type bytefield {
  title: "ELF64 header"
  width: 16
  cell: 40 46
  ruler: on
}

graph { background: #0b1120 }

style field {
  fill: #1e293b
  stroke: #334155 1
  radius: 3
  font: 12 #e2e8f0
}

style magic extends field { fill: #422006 stroke: #f59e0b 1 }
style offset extends field { fill: #0c2a3e stroke: #38bdf8 1 }

// `field <id> ["label"] <bytes> <bytes>` — an inclusive range, in position.
field ident   "e_ident" .magic   0 15
field etype   "e_type"          16 17
field machine "e_machine"       18 19
field version "e_version"       20 23
field entry   "e_entry"         24 31
field phoff   "e_phoff" .offset 32 39
field shoff   "e_shoff" .offset 40 47
field flags   "e_flags"         48 51
field ehsize  "e_ehsize"        52 53
field phentsz "e_phentsize"     54 55
field phnum   "e_phnum"         56 57
field shentsz "e_shentsize"     58 59
field shnum   "e_shnum"         60 61
field shstr   "e_shstrndx"      62 63
```

</details>

Edges and placement are ignored by the chart archetypes — and reported, not
silently dropped.

`style node { … }` is the only text hook a chart has, so it governs the
title, the on-slice labels and the legend alike. On-slice text defaults to
white, which reads on all eight palette hues; everything else defaults to the
theme's ink for the surface.

## Accepted words

**Shapes** — `rect` · `box` · `rectangle` · `stadium` · `pill` · `rounded` · `ellipse` · `circle` · `oval` · `diamond` · `rhombus` · `decision` · `hexagon` · `hex` · `cylinder` · `database` · `db`

Several names denote the same shape; pick whichever reads best.

**Arrow heads** — `solid` · `filled` · `triangle` · `open` · `line` · `thin` · `dot` · `circle` · `none`

Used by `arrow:` on an edge.

**Routers** — `straight` · `direct` · `line` · `ortho` · `orthogonal` · `elbow`

Used by `router:` on an edge.

**Dash patterns** — `solid` · `dashed` · `dotted` · `none`

Accepted by `dash:` and inside a compound `stroke:`.

**Alignments** — `left` · `right` · `center` · `middle` · `top` · `bottom`

Used by `align` in a placement. `left`/`right` for a vertical placement, `top`/`bottom` for a horizontal one, `center` (or `middle`) for either — and the default.

**Flow directions** — `right` · `left` · `down` · `up` · `LR` · `RL` · `TB` · `BT`

Used by `flow:` in `graph { … }`, for nodes that declare no placement.

**Pie labels** — `percent` · `value` · `both` · `none`

Used by `labels:` in `type pie { … }`.

### Categorical palette

Pie slices that declare no `fill` take these hues, in order, never cycled. Two columns of the same eight hues, stepped for a light or a dark `background`; the renderer picks the column from the surface's luminance.

The order is validated: worst adjacent-pair separation is ΔE 9.1 for protanopia on light and 8.4 on dark (OKLab ×100, ≥ 8 target), and 19.6 / 19.3 for normal vision (≥ 15 floor).

| Slot | Light | Dark |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `#2a78d6` | `#3987e5` |
| 2 | `#eb6834` | `#d95926` |
| 3 | `#1baf7a` | `#199e70` |
| 4 | `#eda100` | `#c98500` |
| 5 | `#e87ba4` | `#d55181` |
| 6 | `#008300` | `#008300` |
| 7 | `#4a3aa7` | `#9085e9` |
| 8 | `#e34948` | `#e66767` |

There is no ninth hue. Past eight slices `check` tells you to merge the tail into an `Other` slice rather than repeat a color.

## Diagnostics

`check` and the language server report exactly the same things — one
validator serves both, so the editor can never disagree with the build.

**Errors**

- an unknown property, style, node, shape, router, arrow head or archetype
  (property typos come with a suggestion)
- a node declared twice, or `type` declared twice
- a node named after a statement keyword (`type`, `graph`, `style`, `node`) —
  an edge cannot start with one, so the name would be half-usable at best
- a node anchored to itself, or a cycle of anchors
- a style that extends an unknown style, or extends itself in a cycle
- a property with no value
- `type pie` — a node with no `value`, or a negative one
- `type packet` — a node with no `bits`, or ranges that overlap

**Warnings**

- a property with no effect where it is written (`shape` on an edge,
  `value` outside `type pie`, a setting on an archetype that takes none)
- a style declared more than once
- text whose contrast against what sits behind it is below 3:1
- `type pie` — a slice with value 0; fewer than three slices, which a bar or
  a single number compares better; more than eight, which exhausts the palette
- `type packet` — bits left unassigned between two fields
- an edge or a placement in an archetype that ignores it

## Templates

A `.bd` file may leave holes for a program to fill:

```
type pie { title: "Revenue by region, {{year}}" }

slice emea "EMEA" {{emea}}
slice amer "{{amer_label}}" {{amer}}
```

`{{name}}` parses, so a template stays editable — the editor would otherwise
light up every line of it — and `check` skips the validation that depends on a
value nobody has bound yet.

From the shell:

```
bgraph revenue.bd -o revenue.svg --set year=2026 --set emea=4820
bgraph revenue.bd --emit --set …          # print the filled source instead
```

From Rust:

```rust
use bgraph::{Bindings, Template};

let template = Template::parse(&source)?;
let svg = template.render(
    &Bindings::new()
        .set("year", 2026i64)
        .set("emea", 4820i64)
        .set("amer_label", "Americas"),
)?;
```

A bound value is escaped for **where it lands**: inside a string literal it is
escaped for one, in a value position text is quoted. Blind replacement would
let a stray quote turn a label into a syntax error, or into different
statements. A list spreads space-separated, which is how every list in this
language reads — so `{{points}}` bound to `[10, 20, 30]` fills a whole series.

An unbound hole is an error naming it. Rendering a blank would put a wrong
figure in a document, which is worse than failing.

`Value::Raw` inserts verbatim, and is the only way to fill an identifier or a
colour — both of which would otherwise be quoted as text.

### Repetition

Substitution cannot give a chart a number of items that is not known when the
template is written — a pie with a variable number of slices. So a line that
holds a `{{row.field}}` hole is written **once per row**:

```
type pie
slice {{region.id}} "{{region.name}}" {{region.revenue}}
```

```rust
template.render(&Bindings::new().rows("region", vec![
    Bindings::new().set("id", Value::Raw("emea".into()))
                   .set("name", "EMEA").set("revenue", 4_820i64),
    Bindings::new().set("id", Value::Raw("amer".into()))
                   .set("name", "Americas").set("revenue", 6_310i64),
]))?;
```

The line is the unit because it is the unit the language already uses: a
statement ends at a newline. So "repeat this" needs no block syntax, and there
is no way to get the nesting wrong.

That is deliberately the whole of it — **one line, one list, no nesting and no
conditions**. A line naming two lists is refused when the template is read,
because there is no number of repetitions a reader could predict. No rows
means the line is not written at all: a chart of nothing draws nothing.

Rows come from the library, not the CLI. `--set` binds scalars; a list of rows
is what a document generator has and a shell argument is not.

## Building only what you use

Every archetype is a cargo feature, so a program that needs one chart does not
compile the other fourteen:

```toml
bgraph = { version = "0.1", default-features = false, features = ["pie"] }
```

`free` is not a feature — it is the language itself, and a file that declares
no `type` is a free graph. An archetype that is **not** compiled in is
*unknown*, not broken: `check` reports it and lists what is available, rather
than accepting the file and failing to draw it.

## Editor support

`bgraph-lsp` speaks LSP over stdin/stdout with no arguments, so any client can
use it. A Zed extension is packaged in [`../editors/zed`](../editors/zed)
together with a tree-sitter grammar.

It provides diagnostics, go-to-definition from any reference to its
declaration, a symbol outline, hover (a property's syntax and meaning, a
node's label and **resolved position and size**, a style's flattened property
list), and context-aware completion.

Completion is deliberately quiet: it never fires inside a label or a comment,
`.` only opens the style list where a class reference can actually go, aliases
are hidden, and `value` / `bits` appear only under the archetype that reads
them.

## Grammar

The authoritative grammar is [`../src/syntax.pest`](../src/syntax.pest); the
tree-sitter grammar in [`../tree-sitter-bgraph`](../tree-sitter-bgraph) mirrors
it and is covered by a corpus test suite.

Two details are worth knowing because they shape the syntax:

- Newlines separate statements, so horizontal whitespace and newlines are not
  interchangeable.
- Inside a `{ }` block, a property's value list ends at the next `name:`. That
  is what lets `{ fill: #111 stroke: #222 }` sit on one line.
